paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The calendar is for the next six weeks, from October 7 through November 17, and it covers Sunday dinner plus two weekday meals each week. My sister Lena offered to keep the shared copy on the refrigerator, and I said I could enter changes on my phone after people texted her. We are not changing the old family rule that nobody has to cook on their birthday, and the calendar is only a plan, not a promise.

At the first kitchen meeting, we had six people around the table: Grandma Jo, Aunt Priya, Lena, my brother Marcus, my daughter Ellie, and me. Marcus brought the paper calendar from the pharmacy, and Ellie drew a small leaf beside each Sunday so the kids could see which meal was coming up. Grandma said, “I can make the soup, but only if somebody else carries the big pot.” We all agreed that was fair. The first meeting was on Tuesday—no, Thursday, October 3—because Marcus had written the wrong day in his message. I put Thursday in the notes and changed the calendar before anyone copied it.

We picked the first Sunday meal as lentil soup, bread, and salad at Grandma Jo’s apartment. Lena will bring the bread from the bakery on Pine Street, and I will take the soup pot upstairs because the elevator is slow and the pot is heavy. Ellie asked whether soup counted as a full meal, and Grandma said, “Right,” meaning yes, it does if we also have bread and something fresh. Marcus offered to bring salad, but he cannot shop before six on weekdays, so that offer is only for Sunday. The salad can be whatever greens look good, and we do not need to buy a particular kind.

Then I read out the weekday plan and asked everyone to stop me if a date would not work:
1. On Monday, October 7, Marcus will make chicken rice bowls at his place and set aside one plain bowl for Ellie because she does not want the sauce.
2. On Wednesday, October 9, I will make baked potatoes at home, and people can add beans, cheese, or broccoli.
3. On Monday, October 14, Lena will bring vegetable noodles to Grandma’s, and she will text before leaving so Grandma can meet her at the front door.
4. On Wednesday, October 16, Aunt Priya will make eggplant with couscous, but only if she finds the mild paprika she uses. If the shop has only the hot kind, she will message the group, and we will move that meal to the following Wednesday.
5. On Monday, October 21, there is no shared meal because Marcus has a late shift, and everyone can sort out dinner for themselves.
6. On Wednesday, October 23, Ellie and I will make tomato pasta together at our apartment, and we will keep the cheese in a separate bowl.

After that, we filled in the next two Sundays and checked the family calendar on the wall against the messages on Lena’s phone. Sunday, October 13, is roasted chicken at Aunt Priya’s, and she asked us to arrive at 5:30 rather than 6:00 because her building is testing the fire alarm at 7:00. Sunday, October 20, is chili at my place. I will make one pot with beans and a second, smaller pot without beans for Grandma Jo because beans upset her stomach. Lena said she could bring cornbread, but she has not chosen a bakery yet, so the note just says “cornbread if available.” I asked whether that meant we should buy some if she could not find it, and she said yes, we should keep a small loaf in the freezer as a backup.

For the last four weeks, we left a few choices open because Marcus’s shift schedule comes out late and Priya may have a weekend class. We still entered the dates so nobody would assume those weeks were forgotten. Sunday, October 27, is marked “soup or stew at Grandma’s,” with the cook to be chosen after Marcus gets his schedule. Sunday, November 3, is marked “family leftovers at my place,” and everybody should bring one labeled container if they want to share. Monday, November 4, is a possible meal at Lena’s, but only if she is not working the late shift that day. If she is working late, the meal moves to Wednesday, November 6, and I will update the wall calendar once she confirms. Sunday, November 10, is marked lunch rather than dinner because Ellie has a school concert that evening, and Sunday, November 17, is the final meal in this calendar, but we have not picked a dish yet.

We also wrote down a few practical details under the dates. The person hosting checks whether there are enough plates and clean dish towels before the day. The cook does not have to pay for every ingredient alone, and people can ask the group to bring something simple, such as fruit or milk. If the meal is at Grandma Jo’s, we use the side entrance because the main stairwell door sticks, and the shopping bags should not be left in the hallway. Lena will keep the receipts in the blue envelope on the refrigerator so we can see what the shared food has cost. Nobody is expected to calculate exact portions or settle money that night. If someone has a food allergy, they should tell the cook directly and also put it in the group message so the information does not get lost.

Before we finished, I asked Lena to read the dates back to us. She caught that I had put the potatoes on October 8 in my phone, even though the spoken plan was Wednesday, October 9. I corrected the phone entry, and Marcus checked that his chicken bowls were still on Monday, October 7. Grandma took a picture of the paper calendar and said she would call if the small print was hard to read. We agreed that any change needs a name and a date beside it rather than an erased note, and if the November 4 shift question is still unanswered by October 30, Lena will send a reminder in the group chat. The calendar ends on November 17, and after that we will decide whether to make another one."}]
